89231.m: The flower colour of many hydrangeas depends on how acidic the soil is.

89232.q: What is the dye litmus obtained from?
89232.e: Litmus is a mixture of dyes obtained from certain lichens. It is one of the oldest indicators.
89232.m: The indicator litmus comes from lichens.

89233.q: Why does black tea get lighter when you add lemon juice?
a: The tea dyes act as an indicator and change colour in acid
The lemon juice dilutes the tea a lot
89233.e: Some dyes in black tea react to acid. In acidic conditions the tea therefore looks lighter.
89233.m: Black tea gets lighter with acid because its dyes act as an indicator.

89234.q: What is special about universal indicator?
a: It shows the approximate pH with many colour steps
It only works with hydrochloric acid
89234.e: Universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators. That is why it changes colour in many steps across the whole pH range.
89234.m: Universal indicator shows the pH with many colour steps.

89235.q: Which pH value best matches lemon juice?
89235.e: Lemon juice is clearly acidic. With universal indicator paper you measure a pH of about 2 to 3.
89235.m: With a pH of about 2 to 3, lemon juice is clearly acidic.

89236.q: What colour does universal indicator turn in a strongly acidic solution?
89236.e: The more acidic a solution is, the redder the colour. Strongly acidic solutions with pH 1 or 2 turn it red.
89236.m: Strongly acidic solutions turn universal indicator red.

89237.q: What colour does universal indicator turn in a strongly alkaline solution?
89237.e: As the pH rises, the colour changes through blue to violet. That is why strong alkalis turn it dark blue to violet.
89237.m: Strong alkalis turn universal indicator blue to violet.

89238.q: What is the pH of a neutral solution at room temperature?
89238.e: The pH scale usually goes from 0 to 14. Pure water is neutral and has a pH of 7 at room temperature.
89238.m: Neutral solutions have a pH of 7.

89239.q: A solution has a pH of 3. What is it like?
89239.e: All values below 7 mean acidic. A pH of 3 shows a clearly acidic solution.

89240.q: Solution A has pH 2, solution B has pH 5. Which statement is true?
a: Solution A is more acidic than solution B
Solution B is more acidic than solution A
89240.e: The lower the pH, the more acidic the solution. With each pH step, the concentration of acid particles changes tenfold.
89240.m: The lower the pH, the more acidic a solution is.

89241.q: How do you measure the pH with universal indicator paper?
a: You compare the colour of the paper with a colour chart
You measure how quickly the paper dries
You hold the paper up to the light and count the dots
89241.e: You dip the paper briefly into the solution. Then you compare the colour with the colour chart on the packet.
89241.m: You read the pH from indicator paper by comparing it with a colour chart.

89242.q: Roughly what colour does universal indicator turn in soapy water with pH 9 to 10?
89242.e: Soapy water is slightly alkaline. At these pH values, universal indicator turns blue.
89242.m: Slightly alkaline solutions such as soapy water turn universal indicator blue.

89243.q: What forms when an acid is neutralised with an alkali?
89243.e: The hydrogen ions of the acid and the hydroxide ions of the alkali join to form water. The other ions form a salt.
89243.m: An acid and an alkali react to form salt and water.

89244.q: Which salt forms when hydrochloric acid is neutralised with sodium hydroxide solution?
89244.e: HCl and NaOH make NaCl and H2O. Sodium chloride is our table salt.
89244.m: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution give table salt and water.

89246.q: What do you feel on the beaker when you mix hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution?
89246.e: Neutralisation is an exothermic reaction. Heat is given off to the surroundings.

89247.q: What is the method called where you add an alkali drop by drop to an acid until the indicator changes colour?
89247.e: In a titration you add a solution of known concentration drop by drop. The colour change of the indicator shows the neutral point.
89247.m: A titration tells you how much acid or alkali a solution contains.

89248.q: Why do farmers sometimes spread lime on their fields?
a: To neutralise soil that is too acidic
89248.e: Lime is basic and neutralises acids in the soil. Many plants grow better in soil that is not too acidic.

89249.q: You mix equal amounts of acid particles and alkali particles. Roughly what is the pH of the solution afterwards?
89249.e: When acid and alkali cancel each other out exactly, the solution is neutral. With hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution, the pH is then 7.
89249.m: When acid and alkali cancel each other out exactly, the solution is neutral.

89250.q: Which home remedy can you take for mild heartburn because it neutralises stomach acid?
89250.e: Bicarbonate of soda is weakly basic and neutralises excess stomach acid. Carbon dioxide forms, which is why you often have to burp.
89250.m: Bicarbonate of soda neutralises excess stomach acid.

89251.q: Why does limescale form mainly where water is heated?
a: When heated, the lime dissolved in the water comes out as a solid coating
The lime comes from the metal of the appliance
When heated, dust from the air falls into the water
89251.e: Tap water contains dissolved calcium and hydrogen carbonate ions. When it is heated, carbon dioxide escapes and the lime settles as a white coating.
89251.m: When hard water is heated, limescale is deposited.

89252.q: Which substance is a typical active ingredient in descalers?
a: An acid such as citric acid
An alkali such as sodium hydroxide solution
89252.e: Descalers contain acids such as citric acid or sulphamic acid. Acids dissolve limescale.
89252.m: Descalers contain acids because acids dissolve limescale.

89253.q: Why do you rinse a coffee machine several times with clean water after descaling it?
a: So no descaler ends up in the coffee
89253.e: Leftover acidic descaler would make the coffee taste sour. That is why you run clean water through it several times afterwards.
89253.m: After descaling, rinse thoroughly with clean water.

89254.q: Why does more limescale form in appliances in some regions of Switzerland than in others?
a: Because the tap water there is harder
Because the air there is damper
Because the appliances there are older
89254.e: Water that flows through limestone takes up many calcium and magnesium ions and is hard. Hard water leaves more limescale.
89254.m: Hard water leaves more limescale than soft water.

89255.q: What does it mean when tap water is ‘hard’?
a: It contains a lot of dissolved lime
89255.e: Hard water contains many dissolved calcium and magnesium particles. When it is heated, these form limescale.
89255.m: Hard water contains a lot of dissolved lime.

89256.q: Which kitchen ingredient can you use for descaling?
89256.e: Vinegar contains acetic acid. This dissolves limescale, for example on shower heads or taps.
89256.m: Vinegar descales because it contains acetic acid.

89257.q: Why should you descale a coffee machine regularly?
a: Limescale blocks the pipes and makes heating less efficient
89257.e: Limescale builds up on heating elements and in thin pipes. The appliance then needs more energy and can get blocked.
89257.m: Limescale blocks appliances and wastes energy.

89258.q: Why should you not mix descaler with cleaners containing chlorine?
89258.e: Acids release poisonous chlorine gas from cleaners containing chlorine. That is why such products must never be used together.
89258.m: Never mix acidic cleaners with chlorine cleaners.

89259.q: Which organ does the acidic food mixture go to directly after the stomach?
89259.e: After the stomach comes the small intestine. There the acid is neutralised and the food is digested further.
89259.m: After the stomach, the food mixture goes into the small intestine.

89260.q: Which pH is typical for stomach juice when the stomach is empty?
89260.e: In an empty stomach, the stomach juice is strongly acidic. After eating, the pH rises a little because the food buffers the acid.
89260.m: Stomach juice is strongly acidic in an empty stomach.

89261.q: What is one of the jobs of stomach acid?
a: It kills many germs in food
89261.e: The strongly acidic conditions in the stomach kill many bacteria that enter the body with food. It also helps with digestion.
89261.m: Stomach acid protects against many germs from food.

89262.q: Which nutrient is partly digested in the stomach with the help of acid and the enzyme pepsin?
89262.e: Stomach acid activates the enzyme pepsin. Pepsin splits proteins into smaller pieces.
89262.m: The digestion of proteins begins in the stomach.

89263.q: Why does the stomach not digest itself?
a: A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall
The stomach wall is made of metal
The acid is neutral in the stomach
The stomach completely renews itself every second
89263.e: The stomach lining makes a thick mucus that covers the wall. It keeps the acid away from the cells.
89263.m: A layer of mucus protects the stomach wall from its own acid.

a: Stomach acid gets into the gullet
Too much water in the gut
89264.e: When acidic stomach contents flow back into the gullet, they irritate its lining. You feel a burning behind the breastbone.
89264.m: With heartburn, stomach acid rises into the gullet.

89265.q: What kind of substance helps against too much stomach acid?
89265.e: Basic substances neutralise acids. That is why remedies for heartburn contain basic compounds.

89266.q: Where in the body is the acidic stomach juice made?
89266.e: Special cells in the stomach lining, the parietal cells, release hydrochloric acid. Other cells make mucus and enzymes.
89266.m: Stomach acid is made by cells in the stomach lining.

89267.q: Below roughly what pH do we speak of acid rain?
89267.e: Even clean rain is slightly acidic because carbon dioxide dissolves in it; its pH is about 5.6. If it is lower, we speak of acid rain.
89267.m: Rain with a pH below about 5.6 counts as acid rain.

89268.q: Which gas from burning coal and heating oil contributes especially to acid rain?
89268.e: Coal and heating oil contain sulphur. Burning them produces sulphur dioxide, which turns into sulphuric acid in the air.
89268.m: Sulphur dioxide from coal and oil causes acid rain.

89269.q: Which gases from car engines also contribute to acid rain?
89269.e: In hot engines, nitrogen and oxygen react to form nitrogen oxides. In the air these form nitric acid.
89269.m: Nitrogen oxides from engines form nitric acid in the air.

89270.q: Which damage caused by acid rain did people in Switzerland debate especially hotly in the 1980s?
89270.e: In the 1980s, people argued intensely about damage to trees under the slogan ‘forest dieback’. Acid rain counted as an important cause.
89270.m: Acid rain started the debate about forest dieback in the 1980s.

89271.q: Why are marble statues worn away especially badly by acid rain?
a: Marble is made of lime, which is dissolved by acids
Marble dissolves in water like sugar
89271.e: Like limestone, marble is made of calcium carbonate. Acids slowly dissolve it, so statues lose their details.
89271.m: Acid rain eats away buildings made of limestone and marble.

89272.q: Which measure greatly reduced acid rain in Europe?
a: Filters that remove sulphur from exhaust gases
89272.e: Flue gas desulphurisation in power stations and low-sulphur fuels greatly cut the release of sulphur dioxide. Since then rain has been much less acidic.
89272.m: Removing sulphur from exhaust gases has greatly reduced acid rain.

89274.q: What can happen to fish in lakes that have become very acidic from acid rain?
a: They can die because the water is too acidic
89274.e: Many kinds of fish can only cope with slightly acidic water. In very acidic lakes in Scandinavia, whole fish populations died for this reason.

89275.q: How can you tell that an acid is reacting with limestone?
a: It fizzes and forms gas bubbles
The stone gets hot and glows
89275.e: The reaction produces a gas. The bubbles make the acid fizz on the stone.
89275.m: Limestone fizzes when it comes into contact with acid.

89276.q: How do geologists test in the field whether a rock contains lime?
a: They drip dilute hydrochloric acid on it
They put it in salt water
They hold a magnet to it
89276.e: If the rock fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid, it contains calcium carbonate. This is called the acid test.
89276.m: Dilute hydrochloric acid is used to test rock for lime.

89277.q: What is the chemical formula of calcium carbonate, the main part of limestone?
89277.e: Calcium carbonate is made of calcium ions and carbonate ions (CO3). This gives the formula CaCO3.
89277.m: Limestone is mainly calcium carbonate, with the formula CaCO3.

89278.q: What happens to the shell of a raw egg if you leave the egg in vinegar for a day?
89278.e: Eggshells are mainly calcium carbonate. The acetic acid dissolves the shell, and only the soft skin is left.
89278.m: Vinegar dissolves eggshells, which contain lime.

89279.q: Which rock forms when limestone is changed deep in the Earth by heat and pressure?
89279.e: Under great heat and high pressure, limestone is changed into marble. That is why marble, like limestone, is made of calcium carbonate.

a: Water containing carbonic acid slowly dissolves the limestone
Volcanoes blast holes in the rock
89280.e: Rainwater takes in carbon dioxide and becomes slightly acidic. Over a long time it dissolves the lime and forms hollow spaces.
89280.m: Slightly acidic water dissolves limestone and so forms caves.

89281.q: Which of these substances is also mainly made of calcium carbonate?
89281.e: Chalk, limestone and marble are all mainly made of calcium carbonate. Granite and quartz, on the other hand, are mainly made of silicates.
89281.m: Like limestone, chalk is made of calcium carbonate.

89282.q: Which household product removes limescale from a kettle?
89282.e: Vinegar contains acetic acid. The acid dissolves the limescale, and bubbles of carbon dioxide form.
89282.m: Acids such as vinegar dissolve limescale.

89283.q: Which fruits contain especially large amounts of citric acid?
89283.e: Citrus fruits such as lemons and limes contain a lot of citric acid. It gives them their sour taste.
89283.m: Lemons and limes are rich in citric acid.

89284.q: What is citric acid often used for in the home?
89284.e: Citric acid dissolves limescale. That is why it is used to descale kettles and coffee machines.

89285.q: What does pure citric acid look like at room temperature?
89285.e: Pure citric acid is a colourless to white solid. You buy it as a powder, for example for descaling.
89285.m: Pure citric acid is a white powder.

89286.q: With which living thing is most citric acid made industrially today?
89286.e: Today citric acid is mainly made from sugar using the mould Aspergillus niger. Lemons alone could not meet the demand.
89286.m: Citric acid is made industrially with moulds.

89287.q: What are the salts of citric acid called?
89287.e: The salts and esters of citric acid are called citrates. One example is sodium citrate, which is found in foods.
89287.m: The salts of citric acid are called citrates.

89288.q: What is the citric acid cycle in our cells for?
89288.e: In the citric acid cycle, cells get energy from nutrients. Citric acid is an important substance along the way.
89288.m: The citric acid cycle supplies cells with energy.

89289.q: Why can citric acid remove limescale from a kettle?
a: The acid makes the limescale magnetic
The acid makes the limescale invisible
89289.e: Acids react with limescale. The limescale dissolves and can be rinsed away.
89289.m: Acids such as citric acid dissolve limescale.

89290.q: Where did citric acid come from in the past, before people made it with moulds?
89290.e: In the 18th century, citric acid first came from lemon juice. Today it is mainly made from sugar using moulds.
89290.m: Citric acid was first obtained from lemon juice.

89291.q: Where is ammonia often used as a refrigerant?
a: In artificial ice rinks and large cold stores
89291.e: In large cooling systems such as artificial ice rinks, ammonia is a proven refrigerant. Because it is poisonous, it is hardly used in small household appliances.
89291.m: Large cooling systems such as ice rinks are often cooled with ammonia.

89292.q: What does ammonia gas smell like?
89292.e: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a very sharp smell. You may know the smell from badly aired stables.
89292.m: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a sharp smell.

89293.q: What is a solution of ammonia in water like?
a: Different depending on the time of day
89293.e: In water, ammonia takes up a hydrogen ion. This produces hydroxide ions and the solution becomes alkaline.
89293.m: Ammonia forms an alkaline solution with water.

89294.q: What is the well-known process for making ammonia on a large scale called?
89294.e: At the beginning of the 20th century, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed a process for making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
89294.m: Ammonia is made by the Haber-Bosch process.

89295.q: What is most of the ammonia produced used for?
89295.e: Nitrogen fertiliser is made from ammonia. Without this fertiliser, far fewer people in the world could be fed.
89295.m: Ammonia is the raw material for nitrogen fertiliser.

89296.q: What was the old name for a solution of ammonia in water, often used in the past as a cleaning agent?
89296.e: Spirit of hartshorn is ammonia dissolved in water. Ammonia solution is used, for example, in glass cleaners.
89296.m: Spirit of hartshorn is a solution of ammonia in water.

89297.q: Which ion forms when ammonia takes up a hydrogen ion?
89297.e: Ammonia (NH3) takes up a hydrogen ion and becomes the ammonium ion (NH4+). Ammonium salts are found in many fertilisers.
89297.m: Ammonia and a hydrogen ion make the ammonium ion.

89298.q: Is ammonia gas lighter or heavier than air?
89298.e: Ammonia has a lower density than air. That is why escaping ammonia rises upwards.
89298.m: Ammonia gas is lighter than air.

90165.q: What does an exothermic reaction give off to its surroundings?
90165.e: In an exothermic reaction, energy is released, usually as heat. This makes the surroundings warmer.
90165.m: An exothermic reaction gives off heat to its surroundings.

90166.q: Which process is an exothermic reaction?
90166.e: Burning wood releases large amounts of heat and light. The surroundings get noticeably warmer.
90166.m: Every combustion is an exothermic reaction.

90167.q: What does the Greek prefix ‘exo’ in the word exothermic mean?
90167.e: ‘Exo’ means ‘outside’ or ‘out’ and ‘thermos’ means ‘warm’. So exothermic means that heat is given out.
90167.m: Exothermic means that heat goes out.

90168.q: Where are the products of an exothermic reaction in an energy diagram?
a: Not in the diagram at all
90168.e: The products contain less energy than the starting materials. The difference is given off to the surroundings.
90168.m: In exothermic reactions the products have less energy than the starting materials.

90170.q: Disposable hand warmers contain iron powder. Which reaction provides the heat?
90170.e: When you open the packet, the fine iron reacts with oxygen in the air. This rusting happens very fast and gives off heat.
90170.m: The rusting of iron is also an exothermic reaction.

90171.q: What do you notice when you mix dilute hydrochloric acid with dilute sodium hydroxide solution?
a: Nothing, the temperature stays the same
90171.e: The acid and the alkali neutralise each other. This neutralisation is exothermic and warms the solution.
90171.m: Neutralising an acid with an alkali releases heat.

90172.q: What is the highly exothermic thermite reaction of aluminium and iron oxide used for?
90172.e: The thermite reaction produces liquid iron at over 2000 °C. This can be used to join pieces of rail directly on the track.
90172.m: The hot iron from the thermite reaction is used to weld rails together.

90173.q: Why does a candle flame feel hot?
a: The wax takes in heat from the air
The air is compressed by light
90173.e: The wax reacts with oxygen. This releases energy as heat and light.
90173.m: A burning candle gives off energy as heat and light.

90174.q: What does an endothermic reaction do with energy?
90174.e: An endothermic reaction needs energy from its surroundings, for example heat or light. Without a supply of energy it does not continue.
90174.m: An endothermic reaction takes in energy from its surroundings.

90175.q: Where do plants get the energy for endothermic photosynthesis?
90175.e: Plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water. The energy is stored in the sugar.
90175.m: Photosynthesis needs the energy of sunlight.

90176.q: Instant cold packs get cold after you snap them. What happens inside?
a: A salt dissolves and takes in heat
A gas burns in the bag
90176.e: Inside the bag a salt such as ammonium nitrate dissolves in water. This process takes in heat from the surroundings, so the pack gets cold.
90176.m: A process that takes in heat cools its surroundings.

90178.q: Where are the products of an endothermic reaction in an energy diagram?
90178.e: The products have stored the energy that was taken in. That is why they are higher than the starting materials.
90178.m: In endothermic reactions the products have more energy than the starting materials.

90179.q: Why must the kiln be heated strongly the whole time when making quicklime?
a: Lime gives off a lot of heat
90179.e: Limestone only breaks down into quicklime and carbon dioxide at around 900 °C. The reaction keeps taking in heat and stops without heating.
90179.m: Making quicklime needs a constant supply of heat.

90180.q: Water is split into hydrogen and oxygen with electricity. What happens if you switch the electricity off?
90180.e: The electrolysis of water is endothermic. It needs a constant supply of electrical energy and stops at once without electricity.
90180.m: Endothermic reactions only run with a constant supply of energy.

90181.q: What does the Greek prefix ‘endo’ in the word endothermic mean?
90181.e: ‘Endo’ means ‘inside’ or ‘in’. In an endothermic reaction, heat goes into the system.
90181.m: Endothermic means that heat goes in.

90182.q: What is meant by activation energy?
a: The energy a reaction needs to start
The energy released at the end
90182.e: For particles to react, bonds must first be loosened. The starting energy needed for this is called activation energy.
90182.m: Activation energy gets a reaction going.

90183.q: Where does the activation energy come from when you strike a match?
a: From the moisture in the air
From the light in the room
From the weight of the match
90183.e: Rubbing the match on the striking surface creates heat. This heat starts the reaction in the match head.
90183.m: The heat of friction can start a reaction.

90184.q: Why does a piece of wood on the table not burn by itself, even though oxygen is there?
90184.e: Burning wood does release energy, but it must be started first. At room temperature there is not enough energy for this.
90184.m: Without starting energy, even burning does not begin.

90185.q: How is activation energy shown in an energy diagram?
a: As an energy hill before the products
As a valley below the starting materials
As an arrow pointing down at the end
90185.e: From the starting materials the curve first rises before it leads to the products. The height of this hill is the activation energy.
90185.m: The activation energy is the energy hill a reaction must get over.

90186.q: What provides the activation energy for combustion in a petrol engine?
a: The spark from the spark plug
90186.e: The spark plug makes an electric spark. It ignites the mixture of petrol vapour and air in the cylinder.
90186.m: In a petrol engine, a spark starts the combustion.

90187.q: Why do many reactions happen faster at higher temperatures?
a: More particles have enough energy to start
90187.e: The warmer it is, the faster the particles move. So more collisions reach the necessary activation energy.
90187.m: Heat helps to reach the activation energy.

90188.q: When does a collision between two particles lead to a reaction?
a: When the particles are the same size
When the particles are standing still
90188.e: Only collisions with at least the activation energy are successful. Weaker collisions make the particles bounce apart unchanged.
90188.m: Only collisions with enough energy lead to a reaction.

90189.q: What does a catalyst do to the energy hill of a reaction?
90189.e: A catalyst lowers the activation energy. This makes the reaction start more easily and run faster.
90189.m: A catalyst lowers the energy hill.

90190.q: What does a catalyst do in a chemical reaction?
a: It speeds it up without being used up
It increases the mass of the products
90190.e: A catalyst makes a reaction run faster. At the end it is still there, unchanged.
90190.m: A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up itself.

90191.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
90191.e: The catalyst makes a different reaction path possible, with a smaller energy hill. So more particles react in the same time.
90191.m: A catalyst makes the energy hill smaller.

90192.q: Which poisonous gas does a car's catalytic converter turn into carbon dioxide?
90192.e: Carbon monoxide is very poisonous. In the catalytic converter it reacts with oxygen to form less dangerous carbon dioxide.
90192.m: The catalytic converter turns poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances.

90193.q: Which precious metal works in many catalytic converters?
90193.e: Catalytic converters contain thin layers of platinum, palladium or rhodium. These metals speed up the conversion of the exhaust gases.
90193.m: Platinum is an important metal in the catalytic converter.

90194.q: What are the catalysts in living things called?
90194.e: Enzymes are mostly proteins that speed up reactions in the body. Without them, digestion, for example, would be far too slow.
90194.m: Enzymes are the catalysts of living things.

90195.q: Why does bread taste slightly sweet after you chew it for a long time?
a: An enzyme in saliva splits starch into sugar
The bread gets warm in the mouth
90195.e: Saliva contains an enzyme that splits starch into smaller sugar particles. That is why bread tastes sweetish after long chewing.
90195.m: An enzyme in saliva breaks starch down into sugar.

90196.q: Why does industry use catalysts in many manufacturing processes?
a: The reactions run faster and need less energy
The catalyst becomes the finished product
90196.e: Catalysts speed up reactions, often at lower temperatures too. This saves time, energy and money.
90196.m: Catalysts save time and energy in industry.

90197.q: If you add manganese dioxide to hydrogen peroxide, it foams a lot. Which gas forms?
90197.e: Manganese dioxide acts as a catalyst and speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide. This produces water and oxygen.
90197.m: Manganese dioxide speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide.

90198.q: Where is the catalytic converter in a car?
90198.e: The catalytic converter is built into the exhaust pipe. The exhaust gases flow through it and are turned into less harmful substances.
90198.m: The catalytic converter cleans the exhaust gases in the exhaust.

90199.q: Why does food go off more slowly in the fridge?
a: There is no air at all in the fridge
The light in the fridge kills germs
90199.e: At low temperatures the particles move more slowly. So breakdown and decay happen more slowly.

90200.q: What usually happens to a chemical reaction when you raise the temperature?
90200.e: At higher temperatures the particles move faster and collide more often. That is why most reactions run faster.

90201.q: Why do wood shavings burn faster than a whole log?
a: They have a larger surface area
90201.e: The more finely a substance is divided, the more particles are at the surface. That is where the oxygen can attack.

90202.q: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid. In which acid is it faster?
90202.e: Concentrated acid has more acid particles per volume. So there are more collisions with the metal.
90202.m: A higher concentration speeds up a reaction.

90203.q: What does the rate of reaction tell you?
a: How much the amount of a substance changes per unit of time
90203.e: You measure how much starting material disappears or how much product forms per unit of time. This gives the rate of reaction.
90203.m: The rate of reaction describes the change per unit of time.

90204.q: Why can fine flour dust in the air explode?
a: The huge surface area reacts in a flash
90204.e: Every tiny grain of flour is surrounded by air. A spark can therefore set off an extremely fast combustion, a dust explosion.
90204.m: Fine dust in the air can burn explosively.

90205.q: Why do reactions run faster at higher temperatures?
a: The particles collide more often and harder
90205.e: Warmer particles move faster. There are more collisions, and more of them have enough energy for a reaction.
90205.m: Heat makes particles faster and reactions more frequent.

90206.q: Marble reacts with hydrochloric acid and forms a gas. How can you measure the rate of reaction?
a: Measure the amount of gas produced per minute
Look at the colour of the acid
Measure the length of the glass
90206.e: You collect the gas and read off the volume at fixed time intervals. The more gas per minute, the faster the reaction.
90206.m: The amount of gas per unit of time shows how fast a reaction is.

90207.q: When 10 g of limestone is heated, 5.6 g of quicklime and a gas are produced. How much gas escapes?
90207.e: The total mass stays the same, so the escaping carbon dioxide weighs 10 g minus 5.6 g = 4.4 g.
90207.m: You can work out the mass of an escaping gas from the difference in mass.

90208.q: Matches burn in a sealed jar on a scale. What does the scale show afterwards?
90208.e: In the sealed jar, no gas can escape and none can get in. That is why the mass stays the same.
90208.m: In a sealed container the mass does not change during a reaction.

90209.q: Steel wool is burnt on a scale and is heavier afterwards. Why?
a: The iron has combined with oxygen from the air
90209.e: When it burns, iron combines with oxygen to form iron oxide. The mass of the oxygen is added.
90209.m: When a substance combines with oxygen, it gets heavier.

90210.q: Two substances react completely to form 50 g of product. One of the substances weighed 30 g. How heavy was the other?
90210.e: Both starting materials together must weigh 50 g. So 50 g minus 30 g = 20 g.
90210.m: You can work out the mass of a missing starting material from the mass of the product.

90211.q: 56 g of iron reacts completely with 32 g of sulphur. How much iron sulphide forms?
90211.e: According to the law of conservation of mass: 56 g + 32 g = 88 g of iron sulphide.
90211.m: Add up the masses of the starting materials to get the mass of the product.

90212.q: 12 g of carbon burns completely with 32 g of oxygen. How much carbon dioxide forms?
90212.e: The masses of the starting materials together give the mass of the product: 12 g + 32 g = 44 g.
90212.m: Mass is also conserved when carbon burns.

90213.q: A candle gets lighter as it burns. Where does the mass go?
a: Into gases that escape into the air
90213.e: The wax reacts to form carbon dioxide and water vapour. These gases spread into the air, which is why the scale shows less.
90213.m: When gases escape, a substance seems to get lighter.

90214.q: What must be the same on both sides of a correct chemical equation?
a: The number of each kind of atom
90214.e: In reactions, atoms are only joined up in new ways, not created or destroyed. That is why each kind of atom must appear equally often on the left and right.
90214.m: In a chemical equation, the number of each kind of atom matches on the left and right.

90215.q: Which country did the chemist Antoine de Lavoisier come from?
90215.e: Lavoisier was born in Paris in 1743. He is one of the best-known French scientists.
90215.m: Antoine de Lavoisier was a French chemist.

90216.q: Which old theory about burning did Lavoisier disprove?
90216.e: According to the phlogiston theory, a substance called phlogiston was supposed to escape during burning. Lavoisier showed that burning substances instead combine with a part of the air.
90216.m: Lavoisier explained burning as a reaction with oxygen.

90217.q: What French name did Lavoisier give to oxygen?
90217.e: ‘Oxygène’ means ‘acid former’, because Lavoisier believed the substance was found in all acids. This is also where the chemical symbol O comes from.

90218.q: How did Antoine de Lavoisier die in 1794?
90218.e: Lavoisier collected taxes for the king. During the French Revolution a court sentenced him for this, and he died on the guillotine in Paris.
90218.m: Lavoisier lost his life in the French Revolution.

90219.q: Which measuring instrument was especially important for Lavoisier's experiments?
90219.e: Lavoisier weighed substances very precisely before and after a reaction. In this way he realised that the total mass stays the same.
90219.m: Lavoisier made the precise balance the most important tool in chemistry.

90220.q: As Lavoisier showed, which gas from the air do burning substances combine with?
90220.e: Lavoisier realised that part of the air is used up during burning. He called this substance oxygen.
90220.m: When substances burn, they combine with oxygen.

90221.q: Lavoisier's famous textbook came out in 1789. Which event began in the same year?
a: The founding of the Swiss Confederation
90221.e: The textbook ‘Traité élémentaire de chimie’ came out in 1789. In the same year, citizens in Paris stormed the Bastille.
90221.m: Lavoisier's textbook came out in the year of the French Revolution.

90222.q: What did Lavoisier show about water?
a: It is a compound of two elements
It is an element that cannot be split
90222.e: For a long time water was thought to be a basic element. Lavoisier showed that it can be split and also built up from hydrogen and oxygen.
90222.m: Water is not an element but a compound.

90223.q: Because of his work, what is Antoine de Lavoisier often called?
90223.e: With precise measurements, clear names for substances and the law of conservation of mass, he laid the foundations of today's chemistry.
90223.m: Lavoisier is seen as the founder of modern chemistry.

90224.q: Why are balloons filled with helium today instead of hydrogen?
90224.e: Hydrogen forms an explosive mixture with air. Helium is also lighter than air, but it does not burn.
90224.m: Mixed with air, hydrogen catches fire very easily.

90225.q: How do you hold the test tube for the hydrogen pop test?
90225.e: Hydrogen is much lighter than air and would escape upwards out of an open, upright tube. That is why you hold the opening downwards.
90225.m: Because hydrogen is so light, you hold the tube upside down.

90226.q: How can you tell that the hydrogen pop test is positive?
a: By a whistling or squeaky pop sound
90226.e: The gas burns very quickly in the tube. This makes a typical whistle or a short pop.
90226.m: A whistle or pop in the pop test shows hydrogen.

a: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen
A mixture of nitrogen and argon
90227.e: Oxyhydrogen is made of hydrogen and oxygen. Even a small spark makes it react violently.
90227.m: Oxyhydrogen is an explosive mixture of hydrogen and oxygen.

90228.q: Which substance forms when oxyhydrogen reacts?
90228.e: Hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water. After the test you can sometimes see tiny droplets in the tube.

90229.q: In what ratio by volume do hydrogen and oxygen in oxyhydrogen react most violently?
90229.e: A water molecule needs two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. That is why a mixture of two parts hydrogen and one part oxygen reacts most violently.
90229.m: In oxyhydrogen there are two parts hydrogen to one part oxygen.

90230.q: What do you hear when there is almost pure hydrogen in the test tube?
90230.e: Pure hydrogen burns quietly at the opening, because there is hardly any oxygen in the tube. It only whistles loudly when air is mixed in.
90230.m: Pure hydrogen burns with a quiet sound.

90231.q: Which reaction is often used in the school lab to make hydrogen for the pop test?
90231.e: Base metals such as zinc react with hydrochloric acid. Bubbles of hydrogen rise up.
90231.m: Zinc and hydrochloric acid produce hydrogen in the lab.

90232.q: Why must the valves of oxygen cylinders never be lubricated with oil or grease?
a: Oil can catch fire violently in pure oxygen
Oil blocks the cylinder at once
90232.e: In pure oxygen, substances burn much more violently than in air. Oil and grease can even catch fire by themselves there.
90232.m: Pure oxygen and oil are a dangerous mix.

90233.q: What do you see in a positive glowing splint test?
a: The glowing splint bursts into a bright flame
90233.e: In pure oxygen, wood burns much more strongly than in air. That is why the glowing tip relights with a bright flame.
90233.m: A glowing splint that relights shows oxygen.

a: A wooden splint that glows but does not burn
A metal rod with a battery
A small glass tube with gas
90234.e: You light a wooden splint and blow out the flame. What remains is a glowing tip that only smoulders.
90234.m: A glowing splint is a glowing piece of wood without a flame.

90235.q: Why does a glowing splint not relight in normal air?
a: Air contains only about 21 per cent oxygen
90235.e: To relight, the splint needs much more oxygen than there is in normal air. There it just keeps glowing.
90235.m: Normal air has too little oxygen to relight a glowing splint.

90236.q: What happens to a glowing splint in carbon dioxide?
a: It bursts into a bright flame
90236.e: Carbon dioxide does not support burning. The glowing wood lacks oxygen and goes out.
90236.m: A glowing splint goes out in carbon dioxide.

90237.q: What are substances such as oxygen called that strongly help things burn?
90237.e: Oxygen does not burn itself, but it makes burning much more violent. Such substances are called oxidising.
90237.m: Oxygen is not flammable, but it is oxidising.

90238.q: Which hazard symbol is on cylinders of pure oxygen?
90238.e: The symbol with a flame over a circle marks oxidising substances. It warns that fires can become much more violent.
90238.m: A flame over a circle warns of oxidising substances.

90239.q: In the light, water plants form gas bubbles that relight a glowing splint. Which process makes the gas?
90239.e: Photosynthesis produces oxygen as well as glucose. The plant releases it into the water as bubbles.
90239.m: Plants give off oxygen during photosynthesis.

90240.q: Which gas is detected with the limewater test?
90240.e: You bubble the gas through limewater. If it turns cloudy, that shows carbon dioxide.
90240.m: The limewater test detects carbon dioxide.

90241.q: What do you see in a positive limewater test?
a: The limewater turns milky and cloudy
90241.e: Fine white particles form in the clear limewater. This makes the liquid look milky.
90241.m: If limewater turns cloudy, carbon dioxide is present.

a: A solution of calcium hydroxide in water
90242.e: Limewater is made by dissolving slaked lime, that is calcium hydroxide, in water and filtering it. It is clear and colourless.
90242.m: Limewater is clear, dissolved calcium hydroxide.

90243.q: Which substance makes limewater go cloudy in the limewater test?
90243.e: Carbon dioxide reacts with the dissolved calcium hydroxide to form calcium carbonate. This chalk hardly dissolves and appears as a white cloudiness.
90243.m: In the limewater test, calcium carbonate forms.

90244.q: Roughly how much carbon dioxide does the air you breathe out contain?
90244.e: Air you breathe in contains only about 0.04 per cent carbon dioxide; air you breathe out contains about a hundred times more. That is why limewater goes cloudy quickly when you blow into it through a straw.
90244.m: Breathed-out air contains much more carbon dioxide than breathed-in air.

90245.q: The gases from a candle flame turn limewater cloudy. What does this tell you about the candle wax?
90245.e: The carbon dioxide detected can only form if the fuel contains carbon. The oxygen comes from the air.
90245.m: Carbon dioxide from a flame shows there is carbon in the fuel.

90246.q: Why does limewater go cloudy when you blow into it through a straw?
90246.e: Breathed-out air contains a lot of carbon dioxide. It reacts with the limewater, white chalk forms and the water turns milky.
90246.m: Breathed-out air turns limewater cloudy because it contains carbon dioxide.

90247.q: Is limewater acidic, neutral or alkaline?
90247.e: Calcium hydroxide is a base. Limewater has a pH of about 12 and turns universal indicator blue to violet.

90248.q: When lighting a fire, why does it help to blow gently on the embers?
a: The wind removes the ash as fuel
90248.e: Blowing pushes fresh air onto the glowing parts. With more oxygen, the fire burns more strongly.
90248.m: More oxygen makes a fire burn more strongly.

90249.q: What happens if one side of the fire triangle is missing?
90249.e: All three conditions must be met at the same time. If you remove one of them, burning cannot continue.
90249.m: If one side of the triangle is missing, the fire goes out.

90250.q: Someone pours sand onto a campfire. Which side of the triangle does this remove?
90250.e: The sand covers the embers. No fresh air can reach the fuel any more.
90250.m: Covering a fire smothers it because oxygen is missing.

90251.q: Water is sprayed onto a wood fire. Which condition does this mainly remove?
90251.e: Water takes in a great deal of heat as it warms up and evaporates. The wood cools below its ignition temperature.
90251.m: Water puts out a fire by cooling it.

90252.q: During a forest fire, firefighters cut down trees to make a firebreak. What are they taking away from the fire?
90252.e: In the firebreak there is nothing left that could burn. The fire cannot spread any further there.
90252.m: Without fuel, a fire cannot spread.

90253.q: What is the ignition temperature of a substance?
a: The lowest temperature at which it catches fire by itself
The temperature at which it melts
The temperature at which it freezes
90253.e: Only from its ignition temperature upwards does a substance start burning in air by itself. Every substance has its own ignition temperature.
90253.m: Below its ignition temperature, a substance does not catch fire by itself.

90254.q: You turn off the gas tap on a gas cooker. Why does the flame go out?
90254.e: Without gas flowing in, there is nothing left to burn. The flame goes out at once.
90254.m: Stopping the fuel supply puts out the fire.

90255.q: Why does a candle under an upside-down glass go out after a short time?
a: The oxygen in the glass gets used up
90255.e: The flame uses up the oxygen under the glass. No new air can flow in, so it goes out.
90255.m: A flame constantly needs fresh oxygen.

90256.q: Why must you never put out burning oil in a pan with water?
a: The water turns to steam instantly and throws burning oil out
The water makes the oil colder
The water turns the oil black
The water dissolves the oil at once
90256.e: Water sinks beneath the hot oil and turns to steam explosively. Burning oil sprays everywhere. Instead, you cover the pan with a lid or a fire blanket.
90256.m: Never put out a fat fire with water; cover it instead.

90257.q: Which materials belong to fire class A?
a: Solid materials that form embers, such as wood and paper
90257.e: Fire class A covers solid materials that burn with embers. These include wood, paper, textiles and coal.
90257.m: Wood and paper belong to fire class A.

90258.q: Which fire extinguisher is suitable for computer rooms because it leaves no residue?
90258.e: Carbon dioxide pushes away the oxygen and then evaporates completely. Electrical equipment is not left dirty.
90258.m: A carbon dioxide extinguisher puts out fires cleanly without residue.

90259.q: How does a foam extinguisher put out burning petrol?
a: The foam forms a blanket over the liquid
The foam turns petrol into water
The foam makes the petrol heavier
90259.e: The foam floats on the burning liquid. It separates it from the air and cools it at the same time.
90259.m: A blanket of foam separates burning liquids from the air.

90260.q: Which fire extinguisher works on fire classes A, B and C but leaves a lot of dust?
90260.e: The extinguishing powder works on solids, liquids and gases. Afterwards, though, fine dust lies everywhere and can damage equipment.
90260.m: An ABC powder extinguisher is versatile but makes a lot of mess.

90262.q: What is the best way to put out burning magnesium?
a: With dry sand or metal fire powder
90262.e: Burning metals react violently with water and even with carbon dioxide. Dry sand or special powder smothers the fire safely.
90262.m: Metal fires are put out with dry sand or special powder.

90263.q: Which fire class stands for flammable liquids such as petrol and alcohol?
90263.e: Fire class B covers liquids and substances that become liquid when they burn, such as petrol, alcohol or wax.
90263.m: Burning liquids belong to fire class B.

91087.q: When were most kettle holes in the Swiss Plateau formed?
a: At the end of the last ice age
In the time of the dinosaurs
91087.e: When the glaciers retreated at the end of the last ice age, blocks of ice were left behind in the gravel. When they melted, kettle holes formed.
91087.m: Kettle holes on the Swiss Plateau date from the end of the last ice age.

91088.q: What shape and size are most kettle holes?
a: Roundish and smaller than one hectare
Long and many kilometres in size
Square and as big as a canton
Pointed like a cone and a hundred metres high
91088.e: Most kettle holes are small and roundish. But they can be more than ten metres deep.
91088.m: Kettle holes are usually small and roundish.

91089.q: Where do you find kettle holes?
91089.e: Kettle holes form when glaciers break up. That is why you find them in the foothills of the Alps and in northern Germany.
91089.m: Kettle holes lie in areas from which glaciers have retreated.

91090.q: What often forms when a small kettle lake slowly fills in?
91090.e: Plant remains collect at the bottom of the lake over many centuries. Gradually the lake fills up and a bog forms.
91090.m: Kettle lakes that have filled in often turn into bogs.

a: A lake held back by glacier ice
A lake that freezes in winter
A lake in a volcanic crater
91091.e: A glacier can block a side valley like a dam. Behind it, water collects to form an ice-dammed lake.
91091.m: An ice-dammed lake is held back by glacier ice.

91092.q: Which well-known ice-dammed lake lies at the edge of the Great Aletsch Glacier?
91092.e: The Märjelensee lies in a hollow on the eastern edge of the Aletsch Glacier. In the 19th century it was up to 1.6 kilometres long.
91092.m: The Märjelensee is dammed by the Aletsch Glacier.

91093.q: What holds back the Märjelensee at the edge of the Aletsch Glacier?
91093.e: The Märjelensee lies in a hollow on the eastern edge of the Aletsch Glacier. The glacier ice blocks the outflow like a dam.
91093.m: The Märjelensee is dammed by the Aletsch Glacier.

91094.q: Through which valley did the water drain when the Märjelensee burst in the 19th century?
91094.e: The water drained through crevasses in the glacier and caused floods in the Massa. The Massa flows from the Aletsch Glacier to the Rhône.
91094.m: Outbursts of the Märjelensee caused floods in the Massa valley.

91095.q: Which big river does the meltwater of the Aletsch Glacier flow into?
91095.e: The meltwater flows through the Massa into the Rhône valley. Outbursts of the Märjelensee also caused floods there.
91095.m: The water of the Aletsch Glacier flows into the Rhône.

91096.q: Why is the Märjelensee much smaller today than in the 19th century?
91096.e: The glacier is much thinner today and holds back less water. The natural lake is hardly 100 metres long any more and drains almost every year.
91096.m: Because the glacier is shrinking, the Märjelensee has become small.

91097.q: What is a sudden outburst of a glacier lake called, using a word from Icelandic?
91097.e: In Iceland, dammed glacier lakes often burst. The Icelandic word “jökulhlaup” means roughly “glacier run”.
91097.m: A jökulhlaup is the sudden outburst of a glacier lake.

91098.q: Which huge ice-dammed lake in North America was named after a Swiss scientist?
91098.e: After the last cold period, a huge lake was dammed up at the edge of the North American ice sheet. It was named after Louis Agassiz.
91098.m: The huge Lake Agassiz in North America was an ice-dammed lake.

91099.q: What is a rock glacier made of?
a: Rock debris with ice in between
91099.e: A rock glacier is a mixture of stones and ice. It creeps slowly down the slope like a thick paste.
91099.m: A rock glacier consists of debris and ice.

91100.q: What ground condition does an active rock glacier need?
91100.e: The ice in a rock glacier only remains if the ground is permanently frozen. That is why rock glaciers are typical of permafrost.
91100.m: Rock glaciers exist where there is permafrost.

91101.q: How fast does an active rock glacier typically move?
a: About 10 centimetres to 1 metre per year
91101.e: Active rock glaciers typically creep 0.1 to 1 metre per year. That is much slower than most ice glaciers.
91101.m: Rock glaciers creep only a few decimetres per year.

91102.q: What happens to rock glaciers when the climate gets warmer?
a: The ice inside thaws and the slope can become unstable
91102.e: If the permafrost thaws, the ice between the stones melts. The debris can then creep faster or slide away.
91102.m: Warmth makes the ice in rock glaciers thaw.

91103.q: Why do non-experts often not recognise a rock glacier?
a: The ice is hidden under blocks of rock
It is only visible at night
91103.e: The surface is made of coarse blocks of rock. You cannot see the ice underneath, so it looks like an ordinary scree slope.
91103.m: In rock glaciers, the ice hides under stones.

91104.q: What does a fossil rock glacier that no longer contains ice tell us?
a: That it used to be colder there
That there was a sea there
That there was a desert there
91104.e: Fossil rock glaciers lie outside today's permafrost. They show that there used to be permafrost there, and therefore a colder climate.
91104.m: Fossil rock glaciers are evidence of a colder climate in the past.

91105.q: Where in Switzerland do you find rock glaciers?
a: On the shores of Lake Geneva
91105.e: Rock glaciers need permanently frozen ground. In Switzerland this only exists high up in the Alps, for example in the Engadine.
91105.m: Rock glaciers are found high in the mountains.

a: A cable car up the Titlis
91106.e: GLAMOS stands for “Glacier Monitoring Switzerland”. The network observes and records the changes in Swiss glaciers.
91106.m: GLAMOS measures the changes in Swiss glaciers.

91107.q: Why are Swiss glaciers measured every year?
a: To see how the climate affects them
To turn their ice into drinking water
91107.e: Glaciers react to temperature and amounts of snow. The GLAMOS measurements therefore show how the climate is changing.
91107.m: Glacier measurements show the effects of climate change.

91108.q: How long have the lengths of Swiss glaciers been observed?
91108.e: Systematic observation of glacier lengths began in 1880. The Swiss records are among the oldest in the world.
91108.m: Swiss glacier lengths have been observed for more than 140 years.

91109.q: What happened to the Swiss glaciers in the glacier year 2026?
a: They lost a great deal of ice
They stayed exactly the same size
They moved onto the Swiss Plateau
91109.e: In 2026, more than 5 per cent of the remaining ice melted away. The causes were a winter with little snow and a hot, dry summer.
91109.m: In 2026, the Swiss glaciers lost a great deal of ice.

91110.q: About how many glaciers did the Swiss glacier inventory of 2016 count?
91110.e: The 2016 inventory counted about 1400 glaciers. Many of them are very small, and since 1970 more than 1000 glaciers in Switzerland have disappeared completely.
91110.m: The 2016 glacier inventory counted about 1400 Swiss glaciers.

91111.q: What do glaciologists use to measure how much ice melts in summer?
91111.e: Poles are drilled into the ice, and later scientists measure how far they stick out. This shows how many centimetres of ice have melted.
91111.m: Poles drilled into the ice show how much ice has melted.

91112.q: Why does the glacier year end at the end of September?
a: The summer melt is over by then
It is the coldest day of the year
91112.e: The glacier year runs from 1 October to 30 September. It begins in autumn with new snow and ends when the summer melt is over.
91112.m: The glacier year ends after the summer melt at the end of September.

91113.q: By how much did the ice volume of Swiss glaciers decrease in the five years up to 2026?
91113.e: According to GLAMOS, the ice volume shrank by almost a fifth in these five years. The years 2022, 2023 and 2026 brought especially large losses.
91113.m: In five years, Swiss glaciers lost almost 20 per cent of their ice.

91114.q: What do you call the clear liquid that runs through the filter paper during filtration?
91114.e: Whatever passes through the filter is called the filtrate. It only contains particles small enough for the pores.
91114.m: The liquid that has run through is called the filtrate.

91115.q: What is the solid that stays behind in the filter paper during filtration called?
91115.e: Particles too large for the pores of the filter stay behind in the filter as residue.
91115.m: What gets caught in the filter is called the residue.

91116.q: Which mixture can you separate by filtering?
91116.e: Sand does not dissolve in water; its grains are much larger than the pores in the filter paper and so they get caught.
91116.m: Undissolved solids can be filtered out.

91117.q: Why can’t you filter table salt out of salt water?
a: The salt is dissolved and fits through the pores
The salt is heavier than water
The salt blocks the filter at once
The salt evaporates in the filter
91117.e: When salt dissolves, it breaks up into tiny particles much smaller than the pores of the filter paper. So they run through with the water.
91117.m: Dissolved substances pass through any ordinary filter.

91118.q: Which property of substances is used in filtration?
91118.e: The filter works like a very fine sieve: large particles are held back, small ones get through.
91118.m: A filter separates substances by the size of their particles.

91119.q: What do you call a mixture of a liquid with undissolved solid grains spread through it?
91119.e: In a suspension, solid particles float in a liquid, for example clay in water. Such mixtures can be filtered easily.
91119.m: A suspension contains undissolved solid particles in a liquid.

91120.q: What is a filter paper with many folds, through which liquid runs faster, called?
91120.e: The many folds make the area the liquid can flow through larger. So a fluted filter filters faster than a simply folded paper.
91120.m: A fluted filter has more area and so filters faster.

91121.q: Which piece of lab equipment do you put the folded filter paper into when filtering?
91121.e: The filter paper is placed in a funnel that stands on a container. The liquid runs down through the paper and funnel.
91121.m: When filtering, the filter paper sits in a funnel.

91122.q: In many waterworks, what material is water passed through to filter out suspended particles?
91122.e: Sand filters hold back suspended particles and cloudiness. They are often used in treating drinking water, for example lake water.
91122.m: Sand filters clean water in waterworks.

91123.q: What is the liquid collected after the condenser during distillation called?
91123.e: The vapour turns back into liquid in the condenser and drips into the receiver. This collected liquid is called the distillate.
91123.m: The collected product of a distillation is called the distillate.

91124.q: What is the glass tube surrounded by cold water, in which the vapour turns back into liquid during distillation, called?
91124.e: The Liebig condenser is a double-walled glass tube. Cold water flows on the outside, and on the inside the hot vapour cools and turns back into liquid.
91124.m: In the Liebig condenser, the vapour turns back into liquid.

91125.q: At roughly what temperature does pure alcohol (ethanol) boil?
91125.e: Ethanol boils at around 78 °C, water only at 100 °C. So when a mixture is heated, mostly the alcohol evaporates first.

91126.q: Which substance is distilled off from fermented cherries when making schnapps?
91126.e: Alcohol boils before water. When heated, it evaporates first and is collected in the condenser.
91126.m: When making schnapps, the alcohol is separated off.

91127.q: What do you get as the distillate when you distil salt water?
91127.e: Only the water evaporates and turns back into liquid in the condenser. The salt stays behind in the flask.
91127.m: When salt water is distilled, the salt stays in the flask.

91128.q: Which process is used in a refinery to split crude oil into petrol, diesel and other parts?
91128.e: In the distillation tower, the vapours rise. Parts with different boiling ranges are drawn off at different heights as fractions.
91128.m: Crude oil is split into fractions with different boiling ranges.

91129.q: What is it called when a gas turns into a liquid?
91129.e: In condensation, a substance changes from a gas to a liquid. In distillation, this happens in the condenser.
91129.m: Condensing means vapour turns back into liquid.

91130.q: In a distillation, at what height is the thermometer bulb placed?
a: Level with the side arm leading to the condenser
Right at the bottom in the boiling liquid
91130.e: The thermometer should measure the temperature of the vapour flowing into the condenser. This shows which substance is passing over.
91130.m: In distillation, the thermometer measures the vapour at the side arm to the condenser.

91131.q: What do you do when you decant?
a: Carefully pour off the liquid above the sediment
91131.e: When decanting, you let the solid sink and then carefully pour off the liquid above it.

91132.q: What is the sinking of solid particles in a liquid, which you wait for before decanting, called?
91132.e: Heavier particles slowly sink to the bottom because of gravity. This settling is called sedimentation.
91132.m: In sedimentation, solids settle at the bottom.

91133.q: Which property of substances is used when letting a mixture settle and decanting?
91133.e: Particles with a greater density than the liquid sink to the bottom. This separates the sediment from the liquid.
91133.m: Decanting relies on the difference in density.

91134.q: What do you have to wait for before decanting?
a: Until the solid has settled at the bottom
91134.e: Only when the solid lies at the bottom can you pour off the clear liquid above it.
91134.m: Before decanting, you let the solid settle.

91135.q: What is the glass carafe that wine is poured into when it is decanted called?
91135.e: The decanter gets its name from decanting. The wine is poured in slowly and the sediment stays in the bottle.
91135.m: A decanter is a carafe for pouring wine into.

91136.q: In the lab, what do you let the liquid run down when decanting, so that nothing splashes?
91136.e: A glass rod held at an angle guides the liquid calmly into the new container. That way the sediment is hardly stirred up.
91136.m: A glass rod helps you pour off cleanly.

91137.q: Why is decanting a less clean way of separating than filtering?
a: Fine particles are easily carried along
91137.e: When pouring off, some liquid always stays with the sediment, and very fine, light particles float along. So people often filter afterwards as well.
91137.m: Decanting is quick, but not completely exact.

91138.q: In which part of a sewage works do the undissolved bits of dirt in waste water settle at the bottom?
91138.e: In the primary settling tank, the waste water flows slowly. Undissolved substances sink as sludge, and the water at the top flows on.
91138.m: Sludge settles in the primary settling tank.

a: A substance is dissolved out with a solvent
A substance is evaporated by heat
91139.e: In an extraction, a suitable solvent dissolves certain substances out of a mixture. Other substances stay behind.
91139.m: Extracting means dissolving a substance out with a solvent.

91140.q: Which everyday activity is an extraction?
91140.e: Hot water dissolves colour, scent and flavour substances out of the tea leaves. The leaves themselves stay behind.
91140.m: When making tea, hot water extracts flavour substances.

91141.q: In the school lab, what do you use to dissolve the green leaf pigment out of crushed leaves?
91141.e: Green chlorophyll hardly dissolves in water but dissolves well in alcohol. So the leaves are ground up with methylated spirits or ethanol.
91141.m: Chlorophyll can easily be dissolved out with alcohol.

91142.q: Which piece of lab equipment is used to separate two liquids that do not mix, for example after an extraction?
91142.e: In the separating funnel, the two liquids form two layers. You let the lower layer run out through the tap at the bottom.
91142.m: A separating funnel separates liquids that do not mix.

91143.q: How is sugar obtained from cut-up sugar beet in the sugar factories at Aarberg and Frauenfeld?
a: By soaking it out with hot water
91143.e: The beet slices are soaked in hot water. The sugar dissolves; this raw juice is then cleaned and thickened.
91143.m: Sugar is extracted from the beet slices with hot water.

91144.q: Which property of substances is used in extraction?
91144.e: A solvent dissolves only certain substances well. Because substances dissolve in it to different degrees, they can be separated.
91144.m: In extraction, solubility is what counts.

91145.q: How is caffeine removed from coffee beans to make decaffeinated coffee?
a: By roasting for a long time
91145.e: The beans are treated, for example, with water or with carbon dioxide under pressure. This solvent takes up the caffeine.
91145.m: Decaffeinated coffee is made by extraction.

91146.q: Why do you make tea with hot water rather than cold?
a: Hot water dissolves the substances out faster
Cold water dissolves nothing at all
Hot water makes the leaves bigger
Cold water turns bitter at once
91146.e: In hot water the particles move faster. Colour and flavour substances are therefore dissolved out of the leaves more quickly.

91147.q: In chromatography, what is the solvent that moves through the paper called?
91147.e: The solvent moves and carries the substances with it, so it is called the mobile phase.
91147.m: The mobile phase is the moving solvent.

91148.q: In paper chromatography, what is the paper, which stays in place, called?
91148.e: The paper does not move; it is the stationary, or fixed, phase. The substances stick to it with different strengths.
91148.m: The stationary phase stays in its place.

91149.q: What can you use at home to separate the dyes in a felt-tip pen?
91149.e: You draw a dot on a coffee filter and stand it in a little water. The water rises and separates the dyes.
91149.m: You can separate dyes with filter paper and water.

91150.q: Why do the dyes in an ink separate during chromatography?
a: They stick with different strengths and dissolve to different degrees
They have different weights and sink
They are bleached by light to different degrees
91150.e: A dye that dissolves well in the solvent and sticks only weakly to the paper travels far. Another stops sooner.
91150.m: Substances travel different distances depending on how they stick and dissolve.

91151.q: What often appears when you do chromatography on a black felt-tip pen?
a: It is made of several dyes
It is made of black only
91151.e: Different colours such as blue, yellow and red separate on the paper. Together they look black.
91151.m: Black ink is often a mixture of several dyes.

91152.q: Why do you draw the start line in paper chromatography with a pencil?
a: Graphite does not dissolve in the solvent
Pencil is easier to rub out
Pencil makes the paper more absorbent
91152.e: Ink from a biro or felt-tip pen would travel along too and spoil the result. Graphite stays where it is.
91152.m: The start line is drawn in pencil because graphite does not travel.

91153.q: Why must the start line be above the level of the solvent?
a: Otherwise the samples dissolve straight into the solvent
Otherwise the solvent does not move
Otherwise the solvent evaporates too quickly
91153.e: If the starting spot dips into the solvent, the sample is washed into the container instead of being carried upwards.
91153.m: The samples must not dip into the solvent.

91154.q: What is the result of a chromatography, with its separated spots or bands, called?
91154.e: The finished, dried paper with the separated spots of substances is called a chromatogram.
91154.m: A chromatogram shows the separated substances.

91155.q: What is chromatography used for in laboratories, for example?
91155.e: Chromatography separates mixtures into their parts. This makes it possible to find even tiny amounts of doping substances or poisons.
91155.m: Chromatography helps to detect substances in mixtures.

91156.q: By which property does a centrifuge separate a mixture?
91156.e: Because of the fast spinning, particles with greater density are pushed outwards more strongly. This separates them from lighter parts.
91156.m: A centrifuge separates substances by their density.

91157.q: Which force pushes the heavy particles outwards in a centrifuge?
91157.e: When spinning fast, a centrifugal force acts. It is much stronger than gravity, so separation is quicker than letting things settle.
91157.m: Centrifugal force speeds up separation in the centrifuge.

91158.q: Which part collects at the top of the tube when blood is spun in a centrifuge?
91158.e: The heavier blood cells sink to the bottom. The yellowish, liquid blood plasma stays at the top.
91158.m: When blood is centrifuged, the plasma is at the top.

91159.q: Which kitchen gadget works on the principle of a centrifuge?
91159.e: In a salad spinner, a basket spins quickly. The water drops fly outwards through the holes and the salad stays inside.
91159.m: A salad spinner separates water from salad by spinning.

91160.q: In a dairy, what is separated from milk with a centrifuge?
91160.e: Milk fat has a lower density than the rest of the milk. In the milk centrifuge it collects on the inside as cream and is separated off.
91160.m: A centrifuge is used to separate cream from milk.

91161.q: What must you check before starting a lab centrifuge?
a: Opposite tubes must weigh the same
The tubes must be completely empty
All tubes must have different weights
91161.e: If the centrifuge is loaded unevenly, it starts to wobble and can be damaged. So tubes of equal weight are placed opposite each other.
91161.m: A centrifuge must always be loaded in balance.

91162.q: In which unit do you give how fast a centrifuge spins?
91162.e: The speed is usually given in revolutions per minute. Lab centrifuges often reach several thousand revolutions per minute.
91162.m: Spinning speed is measured in revolutions per minute.

91163.q: Which washing machine programme step uses the principle of a centrifuge?
91163.e: During the spin, the drum turns very fast. The water is pushed outwards through the holes in the drum.
91163.m: During the spin, water is pushed out of the washing.

91164.q: What must you do with long hair before working with a Bunsen burner?
91164.e: Loose hair can get into the flame and catch fire. That is why you always tie it back in the lab.
91164.m: Tie long hair back when using a Bunsen burner.

91165.q: What colour is the Bunsen burner flame when the air hole is closed?
91165.e: Without extra air there is too little oxygen and the gas burns incompletely. The flame is then calm, bright yellow and less hot.
91165.m: With the air hole closed, a yellow, luminous flame burns.

91166.q: What is the hot blue flame with the air hole open called?
91166.e: With plenty of air, the gas burns completely and very hot. The flame is blue and makes a roaring sound.
91166.m: The roaring flame is blue and very hot.

91167.q: Where is the roaring flame of a Bunsen burner hottest?
a: Just above the tip of the inner cone
At the very outer edge of the flame
91167.e: In the inner cone, the gas has not yet burnt completely. Just above it, burning is strongest and the temperature highest.
91167.m: The hottest point is just above the inner cone.

91168.q: How do you set the air hole when you light a Bunsen burner?
91168.e: With the air hole closed, lighting gives a clearly visible, calm flame, and the flame does not strike back. Afterwards you open the air hole as needed.
91168.m: Light a Bunsen burner with the air hole closed.

91169.q: Why is the flame luminous when the air hole is closed?
a: Because of metal in the burner tube
91169.e: When there is too little air, tiny carbon particles form. They glow yellow in the flame and make it luminous.
91169.m: Glowing soot makes the flame yellow.

91171.q: Which gas usually burns in the Bunsen burner in a school lab?
91171.e: Most labs have a natural gas supply. Natural gas is mainly methane; there are also burners for propane or butane from cartridges.
91171.m: A Bunsen burner usually burns natural gas.

91172.q: What do you wear to protect your eyes when working with a Bunsen burner?
91172.e: When heating, liquid can spray or glass can crack. Safety goggles protect your eyes from this.
91172.m: In the lab you wear safety goggles.

91173.q: What do you hold a test tube with when heating it over a flame?
91173.e: The glass gets very hot. A wooden or metal holder grips it safely and protects your fingers.
91173.m: Hold hot test tubes with a holder.

91174.q: Up to what level do you fill a test tube at most for heating?
91174.e: If there is too much liquid in the tube, it can easily shoot out when it boils. A third is a usual upper limit.
91174.m: Fill a test tube only a little for heating.

91175.q: What is the sudden, violent boiling of an overheated liquid, which can make it spray out, called?
91175.e: A liquid can be heated above its boiling point without forming bubbles. Then a lot of vapour suddenly forms and the liquid sprays out.
91175.m: Bumping can throw hot liquid out.

91176.q: How do you hold a test tube when heating it over a flame?
a: At an angle, shaking it gently
91176.e: Tilting and gently shaking spreads the heat evenly. This prevents liquid suddenly spraying out.
91176.m: When heating, hold the test tube at an angle and move it gently.

91177.q: Why does lab glass hardly ever crack when heated?
a: It expands only a little when warm
91177.e: Lab glass is a special glass that hardly expands when warm. So it rarely shatters, even with sudden temperature changes.
91177.m: Lab glass can cope with sudden temperature changes.

91178.q: What do you stand several test tubes in on the lab bench?
91178.e: Test tubes have round bottoms and cannot stand on their own. A rack holds them upright.
91178.m: Test tubes stand in a rack.

91179.q: What do you clean the inside of a test tube with?
91179.e: The long, narrow brush reaches the bottom of the narrow tube. This removes leftovers thoroughly.
91179.m: Test tubes are cleaned with a long brush.

91180.q: What is a conical flask usually made of?
91180.e: Conical flasks are usually made of a special glass that can withstand heat. You can also see clearly what is happening inside.
91180.m: Conical flasks are made of heat-resistant glass.

91181.q: What shape is a conical flask?
91181.e: The flask is wide and flat at the bottom and narrows towards the top into a narrow neck.
91181.m: A conical flask is cone-shaped with a flat bottom.

91182.q: What is the advantage of the narrow neck of a conical flask?
a: You can swirl the contents without spilling
It is easier to pour out
91182.e: Thanks to the sloping sides and narrow neck, hardly anything slops out when swirling. Less also evaporates.
91182.m: A conical flask is good for swirling.

91183.q: Which piece of equipment drips the solution into the conical flask during a titration?
91183.e: The burette is a long tube with a fine scale and a tap. With it you can read exactly how much solution has been added.
91183.m: In a titration, the solution drips from a burette.

91184.q: Why can a conical flask stand on the bench without a stand, but a round-bottomed flask cannot?
91184.e: The round-bottomed flask has a ball-shaped bottom and needs a cork ring or a stand. The conical flask stands safely thanks to its flat bottom.
91184.m: The flat bottom makes the conical flask stable.

91185.q: Which piece of equipment do you use instead of a conical flask to measure an amount of liquid accurately?
91185.e: The scale on a conical flask only gives rough amounts. A measuring cylinder is much more accurate.
91185.m: For accurate volumes you use a measuring cylinder.

91186.q: Why must you never close a conical flask tightly when heating it?
a: The pressure inside could burst it
The liquid would lose its colour
91186.e: When heated, air and vapour expand. In a tightly closed container the pressure rises until the glass can burst.
91186.m: Never heat containers that are tightly closed.

91187.q: What do you do with long hair in the lab?
91187.e: Loose hair can get into a flame or into chemicals. Tied back, it is safe.
91187.m: Long hair is tied back in the lab.

91188.q: What is forbidden while working in the chemistry lab?
91188.e: Chemicals could get onto food or into your mouth. That is why you never eat or drink in the lab.
91188.m: No eating and no drinking in the lab.

91189.q: When diluting a concentrated acid, what do you put into the container first?
91189.e: Mixing releases a lot of heat. If you pour the acid slowly into the water, the heat spreads out and nothing splashes. A rhyme to remember: “Do what you oughta, add acid to water.”

91190.q: How do you check the smell of a substance in the lab?
a: You waft the smell towards you with your hand
You hold your nose right over it
You breathe in deeply over the opening
You taste a little of it
91190.e: Some vapours irritate or damage the airways. By wafting, only a little of it reaches your nose.

91191.q: Where do you work with substances that give off poisonous or sharp-smelling fumes?
91191.e: The fume cupboard sucks the fumes away and carries them outside. That way they do not get into the air in the room.
91191.m: Poisonous fumes belong in the fume cupboard.

91192.q: What do you do first if a chemical splashes into your eye?
a: Rinse the eye with lots of water for a long time
Wait to see if it gets better
91192.e: Rinsing immediately for several minutes with lots of water, for example at the eyewash station, dilutes and removes the chemical. Then you go to the doctor.
91192.m: If a chemical gets into your eye, rinse at once with lots of water.

91193.q: Which emergency number do you call in Switzerland in case of poisoning to reach Tox Info Suisse?
91193.e: Tox Info Suisse gives advice on poisoning around the clock on 145. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 1414 Rega.
91193.m: In Switzerland, number 145 helps with poisoning.

91194.q: Why do you never suck liquids into a pipette with your mouth?
a: The liquid would get too warm
91194.e: When sucking with your mouth, some liquid easily gets into it. So you always use a pipette filler, for example a pipette bulb.
91194.m: Fill pipettes only with a pipette filler.

91195.q: In the lab, what do you use to smother a small fire on someone’s clothing?
91195.e: The fire blanket is wrapped around the person or laid over the fire. It takes the oxygen away from the fire.

91196.q: What are the hazard pictograms on chemicals for?
a: They warn about the dangers of the substance
They show where the substance was made
91196.e: The pictograms show at a glance whether a substance is, for example, toxic, corrosive or flammable. They are the same all over the world.
91196.m: Hazard pictograms warn about the dangers of a substance.

91197.q: What do today’s hazard pictograms on chemicals look like?
a: A black symbol in a diamond with a red border
A white symbol on a green circle
A yellow triangle with a blue border
A black symbol on an orange square
91197.e: Today’s pictograms are squares standing on their corner, with a red border, white background and black symbol. The orange squares are the old symbols.
91197.m: Hazard pictograms are diamonds with a red border.

91198.q: What does the GHS pictogram showing a person’s upper body with a star on the chest warn about?
a: Serious health damage, such as cancer
91198.e: This pictogram stands, for example, for substances that cause cancer, change genetic material or seriously damage the airways.
91198.m: The silhouette with a star warns of serious long-term health damage.

91199.q: What does the GHS pictogram with an exclamation mark mean?
91199.e: The exclamation mark warns of less serious dangers, such as irritation of the skin, eyes or airways.
91199.m: The exclamation mark stands for irritant or harmful substances.

91200.q: Which GHS pictogram do you often find on a drain cleaner?
91200.e: Drain cleaners often contain strong alkalis. The pictogram shows liquid attacking a hand and a surface.
91200.m: Corrosive cleaners carry the corrosive pictogram.

91201.q: What should you do before using a cleaning product with a hazard pictogram?
a: Read the instructions on the label
91201.e: The label says what the dangers are and how to protect yourself, for example with gloves or safety goggles.
91201.m: Always read the label before use.

91202.q: What does the GHS pictogram with a gas cylinder stand for?
91202.e: It marks containers with compressed or liquefied gases. These can burst when heated.
91202.m: The gas cylinder warns of gases under pressure.

91203.q: Which two signal words appear next to the pictograms on GHS labels?
91203.e: “Danger” is used for serious hazards, “Warning” for less serious ones.

91204.q: What did the older hazard symbols look like that were used in Switzerland before the GHS pictograms?
91204.e: As in the EU, orange squares with a black symbol used to be the rule. After a transition period they were replaced by the GHS pictograms.
91204.m: The old hazard symbols were orange squares.

91205.q: When do you wear safety goggles in chemistry lessons?
a: Only when the teacher is looking
91205.e: Splashes and splinters come unexpectedly. So you wear the goggles from the beginning to the end of an experiment.
91205.m: Safety goggles stay on throughout the experiment.

91206.q: What do people who wear glasses put on in the lab for protection?
a: Over-goggles on top of their own glasses
91206.e: Normal glasses have no side protection and are not shatterproof enough. Over-goggles fit over your own glasses.
91206.m: If you wear glasses, put over-goggles on top in the lab.

91207.q: Why do lab safety goggles have side shields?
a: So they do not steam up
91207.e: Chemicals or glass splinters can also get into the eye from the side. The side shields prevent this.
91207.m: Side shields protect the eyes from the side.

91208.q: Why are the lenses of many safety goggles made of plastic instead of glass?
a: Plastic does not shatter on impact
91208.e: Glass can break when hit and throw splinters into the eye. Impact-resistant plastic stays whole.
91208.m: Safety goggles have shatterproof plastic lenses.

91209.q: Which safety goggles protect best against liquid splashes?
